source: Lawson (1979) Cognitive strategies in architectural design, as described in How Designers Think
finding: Block task: final-year architecture students versus postgraduate science students. Scientists tried many block combinations fast to learn the hidden rule (problem-focused). Architects picked blocks for the target colour and swapped in the next best if rejected (solution-focused).
numbers: 3x4 bay single-storey layout, red/blue faces, hidden rules changed per problem, over 6000 possible answers, computer logged strategy. Group sizes not given in this text.
quote: the scientists focused their attention on understanding the underlying rules, the architects were obsessed with achieving the desired result
limits: Textbook retelling, no N, no statistics. The task rewards solution-first search because the computer answers allowed or not allowed. Groups differ in selection and education, not randomly assigned.
agent_relevance: Solution-first versus rule-first is a strategy choice that the environment can reward. Our agent can pick by task: probe the rules when feedback is cheap and rules are hidden.

source: Lawson (1979) first-year replication, in How Designers Think
finding: A second run with school leavers and first-day architecture students found no consistent shared strategy and worse problem solving. Lawson concluded the style comes from degree education, not an inborn cognitive style.
numbers: Two groups: end-of-school pupils and new first-year architecture students. Both were much less good at solving all problems. No consistent common strategy in either group. Cross (2004) states the difference was not found in first-year science and architecture students.
quote: it is the educational experience of their respective degree courses which makes the science and architecture students think the way they do
limits: A null on strategy difference at entry, but also lower overall skill, so the strategy comparison is weak. Cross-sectional, not longitudinal.
agent_relevance: Solution-first is a learned habit, so it can be scaffolded by instruction. Supports putting it in a schema as a taught move, not an assumed default.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Lawson and Lloyd and Scott (1994)
finding: Review confirms the solution-focusing claim and ties it to experience. Lloyd and Scott (1994) found more experienced engineering designers used more generative reasoning, less experienced used more deductive reasoning. Specific experience with the problem type enabled a conjectural approach.
numbers: Lloyd and Scott (1994) protocol study of experienced engineering designers. No N given in the review.
quote: It is the variable of specific experience of the problem type that enables designers to adopt a conjectural approach to designing
limits: Review summary of protocol studies. Small samples. Moderator is problem-type familiarity, not generic seniority.
agent_relevance: Memory angle: solution conjectures work when the agent has retrieved a close precedent. Without relevant memory, forced early conjectures may just be guesses.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Christiaans and Dorst (1992) junior vs senior industrial design students
finding: Junior students gathered little information and solved a simple problem. Senior students split in two. The more creative group asked for less information, processed it at once and set priorities early. The other group gathered lots of data, which became a substitute for designing.
numbers: Protocol study of junior and senior industrial design students. Sample sizes not given in the review.
quote: gathering data was sometimes just a substitute activity for actually doing any design work
limits: Secondhand through Cross. Creativity judged by quality of solutions.
agent_relevance: More research is not better. A cap on information gathering and early priority setting beat open-ended retrieval for the more creative group.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Atman et al. (1999) freshman vs senior engineering
finding: Among freshmen, those who spent a large share of time defining the problem did not produce quality designs. Among seniors, more problem scoping (more and wider information) did give better designs. Overall quality related to rapid alternation between design steps.
numbers: Protocol analysis of freshman (no design experience) and senior engineering students. Sample sizes not in the review.
quote: those subjects who spent a large proportion of their time defining the problem did not produce quality designs
limits: Expertise moderates the value of problem-first work. Reverses a simple rule that problem scoping is always good. Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Problem-first helps only if the scoping is skilled. For a weak scoper, early solution probes may be safer. Test by arm: scope-first vs conjecture-first by task familiarity.

source: Kruger and Cross (2006) Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes
finding: Protocol study found four strategies: problem driven, solution driven, information driven, knowledge driven. Per a search summary and a later paper, solution-driven designers had higher creativity but lower overall quality, and problem-driven designers gave the best balance of quality and creativity. Strategy did not map simply onto quality.
numbers: Exact N and scores not seen. Lemons et al. (2011) restate: solution driven design produced low overall quality, problem driven gave relatively good results.
limits: Not opened (publisher and repository blocked). Numbers unverified. This appears to cut against the claim that solution-first is the expert advantage.
agent_relevance: Solution-first is not free: it may trade quality for novelty. A schema should pair a fast conjecture with a problem-space check before commit.

source: Lemons, Carberry, Swan (2011) Cognitive styles and design strategies of engineering students during a hands-on model-building design task
finding: Qualitative reuse of the Kruger and Cross four-strategy scheme with engineering students. Six of ten were problem driven, three solution driven, one information driven. Solution-driven students had very short problem analysis. Problem-driven students expanded the problem space and used more design features and criteria.
numbers: N=10 students, hands-on model-building task. 6 problem driven, 3 solution driven, 1 information driven. Authors judged solution-driven not optimal for these students.
limits: Tiny qualitative sample, no inferential statistics. Students not experts, so it does not test the expert solution-first claim.
agent_relevance: Most novices default to problem-driven, not solution-first. Supports the view that solution-first is a trained expert style.

source: Morozov, Kilgore, Atman (2007) Breadth in design problem scoping: using insights from experts to investigate student processes (ASEE)
finding: Same river retaining-wall problem given to 124 first-year students (written list) and 4 experienced engineers (think-aloud). Novices listed more natural and social factors. Only two of four experts showed a clear top-down breadth-first approach.
numbers: Novices n=124, 1418 segments, 11.5 statements on average. Experts n=4, 228 segments, 57 statements on average. Experts averaged 19 years of experience (range 7-32). Coder agreement 77% on one transcript, 72% across all four.
limits: Different data collection (written versus think-aloud), so groups cannot be compared directly. Four experts. Authors say comparison is only rough.
agent_relevance: Experts do not reliably scope broadly first. Do not assume the expert pattern is breadth-first problem scoping.

source: Morozov et al. (2007) Table 7 expert vs novice distribution
finding: Frame-of-reference mix was similar for the two groups. Novices gave more natural factors (30% vs 18%) and fewer social (18% vs 24%) and technical (24% vs 30%) ones.
numbers: Design detail 48% novices vs 46% experts. Design context 52% vs 54%. Logistical 27% vs 28%. Wall location 50% vs 46%. Surroundings 12% vs 22%.
limits: Percent shares of coded segments, no significance tests. Experts n=4.
agent_relevance: Overall breadth profile was close between groups. Differences are in what is attended to (technical, existing solutions, alternatives), not how wide.

source: Ball, Ormerod, Morley (2004) Spontaneous analogising in engineering design: a comparative analysis of experts and novices
finding: Experts analogised more than novices (32.2 vs 22.9 analogies per hour). Experts used mostly schema-driven analogies, novices mostly case-driven ones, a crossover.
numbers: N=16 (8 experts, 8 novices). Experts at least 7 years experience (mean 15.1). Novices masters students, mean 3.5 years. Expertise main effect F(1,14)=5.04, p=.041. Form main effect F(1,14)=31.24, p<.001. Interaction F(1,14)=111.33, p<.001. Schema-driven: experts 53.1/h, novices 16.5/h. Case-driven: experts 11.3/h, novices 29.4/h.
limits: One brief (automated rent-a-car facility), 40 to 75 minutes, small N. Novices were advanced students. Most case-driven analogies used surface cues.
agent_relevance: Experts retrieve abstract schemas, novices retrieve concrete cases. For agent memory: store abstract solution schemas as well as cases; case recall by surface match is the novice route.

source: Chen, Chen, Yang (2022) Behaviors of novice and expert designers in the design process: from discovery to design (Int. J. Design)
finding: Mostly null. No significant expert-novice difference in general phase sequence or total time per phase. Differences were in the early stage and then later: experts stayed in the design phase, novices moved between phases more.
numbers: 4 experts vs 5 novices, alarm design for the elderly (protocol analysis, Mann-Whitney U). Longest continuous design activity: experts 976 s vs novices 446 s (significant). Backward transitions during constant design activity: experts 100% vs novices 74%, p=0.06 (not significant).
quote: No significant differences were found between the experts and the novices in terms of the general sequence and the total time spent on each phase
limits: Very small samples, one task, authors say it is inappropriate to conclude much from the indicators. A weak or failed test of the claim that process shape differs by expertise.
agent_relevance: Process-shape metrics (time per phase) may not separate experts from novices. Check agent traces on depth and persistence in the design phase instead.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Ball and Ormerod (1995) and Guindon (1990): rival to opportunism
finding: Guindon found designers interleave problem specification with solution development and called deviations from top-down a natural result of ill-structured problems. Ball and Ormerod found expert electronics engineers deviated little from top-down breadth-first, except for brief depth-first checks of a solution idea.
numbers: Studies of software designers (Guindon) and expert electronics engineers (Ball and Ormerod). Sample sizes not given in review.
quote: Much of what has been described as opportunistic behavior sits comfortably within a structured top-down design framework
limits: Competing explanations: opportunism as cognitive-cost saving (Guindon) versus structured alternation of breadth and depth (Ball and Ormerod). Experiments that discriminate them are not in the review.
agent_relevance: Brief depth-first probes inside a breadth-first plan is a testable agent pattern: keep the plan, allow short solution probes.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on novice depth-first vs expert breadth-first
finding: Novices are usually described as depth-first and experts as top-down breadth-first, but Cross calls this too simple. Ball and Ormerod say experts use a flexible mix: depth-first lowers cognitive load, breadth-first lowers commitment.
numbers: Qualitative review claim. Also notes creative experts treat tasks as ill-defined and solve similar tasks from first principles rather than recalling earlier solutions.
quote: creative experts treat problems as harder problems than novices do
limits: Standard expertise results come from well-defined tasks (chess, physics); design may not follow them. Based on a few studies of writing, programming and design.
agent_relevance: Do not copy the physics expert-novice model into the agent. For open design tasks the expert move may be to make the problem harder, not easier.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Jansson and Smith (1991) fixation
finding: Senior student and professional mechanical engineers shown an example solution reproduced many more features of it than controls. Fixation hit experienced people too.
numbers: Example-brief groups versus plain-brief controls. Counts not given in review.
limits: Secondhand. Original not opened here. Subfield 07 covers it in depth.
agent_relevance: Solution conjectures can anchor. If the agent conjectures first, the first conjecture should be treated as a hypothesis and not shown back as an example.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Purcell and Gero (1991-96) engineers vs industrial designers
finding: Mechanical engineers were more affected by an example design than industrial designers. With an innovative example, engineers fixated on its principle. Industrial designers varied widely either way (fixated on being different).
numbers: Series of experiments with senior mechanical engineering and industrial design students. Numbers not in review.
limits: Authors suggest the effect is due to educational program. A boundary condition: fixation depends on training and type of example.
agent_relevance: Training can shift the failure mode. Fixation and diversity-seeking are both learnable biases; the agent's prompt shapes which one it shows.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Smith and Tjandra (1998) willingness to scrap first concept
finding: In a design game the top three of nine groups were the three that scrapped their first design and started afresh.
numbers: Nine groups of four senior industrial engineering students, artificial triangle-configuration task with four roles.
quote: The top three designs . . . were the three groups that chose to scrap their initial design
limits: Role-play game far from real design. Contrasts with Rowe, Ullman and Ball et al. who saw designers patch bad concepts rather than drop them.
agent_relevance: Discriminating test for the agent: does dropping the first conjecture after a failed check raise accuracy? Fits our revise-state ideas.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on attachment to early concepts (Rowe 1987; Ullman 1988; Ball 1994; Guindon 1990)
finding: Experienced mechanical engineers, senior electronics students and software designers pursued one proposal, patched major problems and avoided rejecting it. Software designers adopted a kernel solution very early and rejected alternatives by trade-off on one criterion.
numbers: Protocol and case studies. No sample sizes in review.
quote: designers typically pursue only a single design proposal
limits: Descriptive, no controls. Cross notes it may reflect satisficing or fluent modification, not error.
agent_relevance: Solution-first has a known cost: commitment. The agent needs a rule to abandon a conjecture after a failed check.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on Akin and Akin (1996) expert vs novice insight
finding: An experienced architect broke out of a standard frame because he had procedural knowledge for a new one. The non-architect novice produced only a conventional solution.
numbers: Case comparison of one experienced architect and one non-architect on a simple architecture problem.
limits: Two participants. Anecdotal.
agent_relevance: A new frame needs a procedure to use it. Reframing prompts without domain procedures may not help weak models.

source: Cross (2004) design cognition review on modal shifts (Akin and Lin 1995; Cross et al. 1994; Atman 1999)
finding: Novel design decisions co-occurred with rapid alternation between drawing, examining and thinking (6 of 8 times). More creative students alternated between gathering information, sketching and reflecting.
numbers: Akin and Lin: single experienced engineering designer, 6 of 8 novel decisions in triple-mode periods. Cross et al. and Atman et al.: student protocol studies, no counts in review.
limits: Correlational, one designer for the key count. Authors caution against causal reading.
agent_relevance: Alternation between modes may be a better process marker than any fixed order. Test mode-switch rate in agent traces.

source: Crismond and Adams (2012) The Informed Design Teaching and Learning Matrix
finding: Literature integration (not meta-analysis) contrasting beginning and informed designers on nine strategies. Beginning designers work with few or one idea and get fixated, treat tasks as well-defined, and propose superficial ideas. Informed designers are midrange, not experts. Lists teaching moves such as building to learn and generating many ideas.
numbers: Nine design strategies. Expertise noted to take 10 or more years (Hayes 1989). No effect sizes.
limits: Review of heterogeneous studies; no pooled effects. Midrange informed level is a proposed construct. Matrix is not validated as a causal intervention.
agent_relevance: A ready-made contrast list of beginner versus informed behaviours that could be coded in agent traces.

source: Mehalik and Schunn (2006) What constitutes good design? A review of empirical studies of design processes (as cited by Lemons et al. 2011)
finding: A review of forty studies, reported second-hand, found that how a problem was construed changed which design aspects were stressed and which solution paths were chosen. Experienced designers spent more time exploring and building several representations of the problem.
numbers: Forty studies, per Lemons et al. No effect sizes seen.
limits: Not opened; only cited. Do not quote figures.
agent_relevance: Problem representation is the main thing experience changes. Memory could store representations, not just solutions.

source: Zhang and Ma (2021) Designing in complexity: how solution conjectures inform problem exploration (ICED21)
finding: Grounded-theory model of how conjectures change problem views: trigger (analogizing, inspiring, evaluating, questioning), problem-space expansion, then incremental or radical adjustment of problem focus.
numbers: Ten multidisciplinary graduate students, interviews and documents, complex real-world problems.
limits: Interview-based, no outcome measures, students not experts. Authors note embarrassment about early conjectures and a concern for novices.
agent_relevance: Gives four ways a conjecture can open the problem. Could be coded as steps in a conjecture-to-reframe loop and tested for effect.

source: Chen, Song, Zheng, Jing, Hansen, Sun (2025) Understanding design fixation in generative AI (arXiv 2502.05870)
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-4o) chair design text was less diverse than Red Dot award designs: 67.4% unique terms vs 78.2%. Four fixation patterns: descriptive statements, repetitive theme, limited contextual variation, susceptibility to high-frequency words. Midjourney images were also less diverse by CLIP distance.
numbers: 10 novice designers (age 20-26, under 1 to 6 years of experience) made 96 solutions. Baseline: 105 Red Dot office chair entries. Structural keywords per 100 cases: Red Dot 208.57 vs ChatGPT 142.71. Unique word items: 312 vs 180. Shared: 86.
limits: Different baselines (award entries versus participant-AI outputs), no between-group test for text, small N, only novice users, only GPT-4o and Midjourney. Novelty measured by word-type overlap, a crude proxy.
agent_relevance: LLM outputs show fixation that looks like the human kind. Solution-first LLM conjectures should not be assumed diverse; test it.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou, Velloso (2024) The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking (CHI)
finding: Between-participants experiment with three arms. Seeing AI-generated images raised fixation on a given example more than image search or no support, and lowered fluency, variety and originality compared with the baseline.
numbers: N=60 (three conditions: no support, Google image search, Midjourney V4). Bayesian multilevel model. Fixation effect: GenAI mean .32 (89% CI .11 to .54), Bayes Factor 124. Image search .27 (CI .05 to .48), BF 42.48. NASA-TLX did not differ, F(2,57)=1, p=0.37.
limits: Participants were mostly students, not experts. Visual sketching task with an example avatar. Image generator, not a text LLM reasoning agent.
agent_relevance: Showing a strong generated example before the agent has its own conjecture raises fixation. Order matters: own conjecture first, then outside samples.

source: Ege, Ovrebo, Stubberud, Berg, Elverum, Steinert, Vestad (2025) ChatGPT as an inventor (AIEDAM)
finding: GPT-4 acting as the designer, with two humans executing, ranked second of six teams in a 48-hour hackathon (NERF launcher distance 14.8 m vs mean 12.0 m). It was strong at concept generation but abandoned promising concepts early, added complexity and showed design fixation.
numbers: Five graduate engineering teams plus one ChatGPT team, over 100 prototypes. Distances: winner 37 m, ChatGPT 14.8 m, then 8.1, 6.6, 5.1, 0.1 m. 20 of 97 prompts were questions and clarifications.
quote: ChatGPT experiences and is limited by design fixation
limits: One event, one task, one run, ChatGPT team had one year more experience, very few teams. Not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Both failure modes appear in one LLM run: clinging to a working concept and dropping a good one early. A schema needs a persistence rule and an abandonment rule.

source: Ege et al. (2025) key finding on novice-like fixation, citing Purcell and Gero (1996)
finding: Authors compare the LLM to a novice designer that clings to one concept. It also fixated on the last item in a materials list inside the prompt, so the team replaced the list with a general description.
numbers: Observation in prompts during pilot and hackathon; no counts. Key finding KF 9.
quote: Much like a novice designer, ChatGPT clings to one concept and is reluctant to try something else
limits: Qualitative observation, prompt-order effect shown by example only.
agent_relevance: Prompt hygiene: order of listed options can drive the output. Randomise or summarise lists.

source: Krajcer et al. (2026) ChatGPT in ideation for UX design students (Design Science; abstract page of TU Delft record)
finding: Within-group study of 35 UX design students found ChatGPT gave convenience and speed but dampened cognitive engagement, which may raise reliance and reduce creative confidence.
numbers: N=35, 214 concepts with and without ChatGPT, expert creativity ratings. No numbers on the page.
limits: Abstract only. A search summary of the earlier thesis said no significant creativity difference; not verified. Numerical results, effect sizes and expertise breakdown not seen.
agent_relevance: Novices lose engagement when the tool does the conjecturing. This is about human users, not the agent.
